description: Gaayhllga Jaad, the Flood Tide Woman, belongs to the Haida tradition of a great deluge. In the story told by Chief Young of Haida Gwaii, a woman wrapped in an unfamiliar fur cape was mocked by children; as she sat by the shore the water rose, sweeping away villages and scattering the survivors on crude rafts. Geologists read the tale as a distant memory of post-glacial sea-level rise.
source: Patrick Nunn, 'The Edge of Memory' (polis-sea.org); Haida oral tradition (Chief Young)
research_notes: Attested. Confirmed via Patrick Nunn's discussion of the Haida flood legend told by Chief Young of Haida Gwaii, framed as oral memory of rapid sea-level rise about 12,700 years ago. The record's claim that she 'controls the tides' is an over-reading; the attested role is the flood-causing woman whose humiliation raises the sea. Cultural attribution Haida / Haida Gwaii confirmed.

description: Nang Kílslaas, 'The One Whose Voice is Obeyed,' is the Haida name for Raven, the creator-transformer who shaped Haida Gwaii and stole the sun, moon, stars, and fresh water to bring them to the world. Raven shifts freely between human, animal, and object forms, and the Xuuya Kaagang.ngas, or 'Raven Traveling' stories, record his many journeys and tricks.
source: Haida Nation (haidanation.com); Ravencalling Productions; Haida oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Nang Kílslaas is the official Haida Nation rendering of the Raven name, meaning 'The One Whose Voice is Obeyed.' He is the central creator/transformer who stole light and reshaped the islands; shape-shifting into a pine needle, a human child, or a woman, unrestricted by species or gender. The record's summary (stole sun, moon, stars, freshwater) matches the Haida cycle.

description: Malahas, the Woman of the Woods in Nuu-chah-nulth tradition, lures children into the forest and is a standing threat to village families. In the myth cycle she steals the children of a woman of the lineage; the hero Andaokut, born from that woman's tears or mucus, later finds her and kills her, returning the children. Malahas is thus central to stories of forest danger and rescue.
source: Wikipedia 'Nuu-chah-nulth mythology' (Malahas)
research_notes: Attested. Malahas is the Nuu-chah-nulth 'Woman of the Woods' who abducts children and is defeated by Andaokut (Wikipedia, Nuu-chah-nulth mythology). Corrected: the record claimed a 'wolf-like creature that aids or tests heroes'; the attested figure is a child-stealing ogre-woman. She is a female wild-woman figure akin to the Northwest Coast wild-woman class.

description: Iqesqes, the Blue Jay, is the trickster hero of Chinook, Chehalis, and Quinault stories along the lower Columbia. Benevolent but foolish, he stumbles through adventures with slapstick results, visiting the land of the dead in the tale of Blue Jay and Ioi, finding a wife, and helping recover the stolen sun. His bungling often sets things right by accident.
source: native-languages.org (Iqesqes/Bluejay); World History Encyclopedia (Blue Jay)
research_notes: Attested. Iqesqes (Bluejay) is a genuine trickster hero of the Chinookan and nearby Salish groups, notable for foolish but good-hearted mischief; documented tales include 'Blue Jay Visits Ghost Town,' 'Blue Jay Finds a Wife,' and 'How The Sun Was Stolen.' The record's 'spirit world' emphasis matches his famous visit to the land of the dead.

description: Boqs is the wild man of the woods in Bella Coola (Nuxalk), Chinook, and Salish tradition, a shaggy forest being of great strength. In Nuxalk and northern Salish versions he is a malevolent cannibal who may harm or abduct people, while some Chinook stories treat him more lightly as a strong but foolish wild man. Popular writing sometimes equates him with the Sasquatch.
source: native-languages.org (Boqs/Bukwus, Wild Man of the Woods); Bella Coola and Chinook oral tradition
research_notes: Attested, with a caveat. Boqs (Bukwus/Bokwus) is the wild man of the woods documented for the Bella Coola/Nuxalk and neighboring Chinook and Salish peoples. In more northern, Bella Coola versions he is malevolent and cannibalistic; in Chinook/Salish versions he is more benign, and 'Skookum' (Chinook Jargon 'big/powerful') is related. The 'defeated by clever young heroes' detail in the record is not specifically documented.

description: In the Chinook texts recorded by Franz Boas, the dead live in a shadowy town where they appear as skeletons and whisper in the dark. The tale of Blue-Jay and Ioi tells how Blue-Jay's dead sister Ioi is taken as a ghost bride at night, and how Blue-Jay travels to the afterworld to bring her back, only to see the dead fall to pieces at dawn.
source: Franz Boas, 'Chinook Texts' (1894), tale 15 (Blue-Jay and Ioi)
research_notes: Attested. Boas's Chinook Texts, story 15 'Blue-Jay and Iô'i,' documents the Chinook land of the dead as a town of bones and skulls where ghosts whisper; Blue-Jay visits his dead sister and marries a ghost bride. The record's 'afterworld visited by heroes seeking lost loved ones' is an accurate summary of this cycle.

description: In the Tlingit Raven cycle, Fish Hawk (the osprey) appears in a folk-etymological tale of how the osprey gained its white head. Raven, in the shape of a woman, marries a chief, and supernatural power from a shaman turns Fish Hawk's head white; the episode also frames Raven's theft of the sun. The bird's keen sight and pale head are thus explained.
source: ANKN/UAF curriculum, 'Raven Stories V: Raven's Greed' (The Raven and the Fish Hawk)
research_notes: Attested. The Tlingit story 'The Raven and the Fish Hawk' (ANKN/UAF Raven Stories V) is a folk-etymology tale: Raven, in the form of a woman, is Fish Hawk married to a chief; a shaman's power gives the osprey its white-feathered head, and Raven later steals the sun. Corrected: the record's 'keen-eyed bird spirit who aids Raven' is a weak gloss; Fish Hawk is a character in Raven's escapade, not a helper.

description: Matlose is a hobgoblin of Nuu-chah-nulth tradition, described in early accounts as a Caliban-like spirit of the woods. His head is said to be only half like a man's, his body horrid with black bristles, his teeth monstrous, and his hands armed with bear-like claws. His voice fells listeners, and a single stroke of his claw rends his prey.
source: Edward S. Curtis, 'The North American Indian'; Wikipedia 'Nuu-chah-nulth mythology' (Matlose)
research_notes: Attested. Matlose is a documented Nuu-chah-nulth hobgoblin, characterized in early accounts (Curtis) as 'the very Caliban of spirits,' with a barely human head, black bristled bulk, monstrous teeth, and bear-claw nails; his voice strikes hearers to the ground. The record's 'mischievous forest being who plays tricks' softens a genuinely terrifying figure.

description: The myth of the Flying Africans tells how enslaved Igbo captives, landing at Ebos Landing on St. Simons Island in Georgia in 1803, turned and walked back across the water to fly home to Africa rather than live in bondage. Collected by the Federal Writers' Project in the 1930s, the tale of flight became a lasting symbol of resistance and freedom.
source: New Georgia Encyclopedia (Ebos Landing); WPA Federal Writers' Project field records
research_notes: Attested. The Flying Africans myth is documented at Ebos Landing, Dunbar Creek, St. Simons Island, Georgia, with a historical root in the 1803 Igbo captive rebellion; variants were recorded by the Federal Writers' Project (e.g., Drums and Shadows). The record's summary (symbol of resistance; WPA collection) is accurate.

description: In Lushootseed tradition of the southern Coast Salish, the Blue Heron is one of the myth-age beings remade by the Changer. In the Puyallup telling, the Changer finds Blue Heron splitting cedar for a canoe, striking the wood with his head and beating it with his hand while singing 'hand, hand, side of the head'; the encounter fixes the heron's form.
source: Puyallup Tribal Language Program (Dukʷibəɫ yəxʷ tiiɫ sbəq'ʷəʔ, 'Changer and Blue Heron')
research_notes: Attested. The Puyallup Lushootseed text 'Changer and Blue Heron' documents Blue Heron as a myth-age being who splits cedar with his head and hand; the Changer (Dukʷibəɫ) reshapes him. Related great-blue-heron material appears in Coast Salish sources (e.g., '#een'thu smuqw'a'). The record's generic 'animal-spirit' gloss is thin but the figure is genuine.

description: Raven is the great transformer-trickster of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a being who reshapes the world through appetite and deception. In the tale of Great-Inventor recorded by Boas, Raven tricks the water-woman of Bull Harbor, fills a bladder with stolen water, and urinates to create the rivers. He also works to release daylight and fix the order of things.
source: Franz Boas, 'Kwakiutl Tales' (1910), story 14 (Great-Inventor)
research_notes: Attested. In Kwakwaka'wakw tradition Raven appears as a transformer-trickster; Boas's 'Kwakiutl Tales' story 14 'Great-Inventor' (dictated by MalE'd, 1893) has Raven under the transformer name Kwekwaxa'we tricking the Bull Harbor water-woman and urinating to make rivers. The record's 'connects to the spirit world' gloss is fair; the core deeds are the river/water theft and transformation.

description: Tseiqami is the thunderbird of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a colossal supernatural bird whose wingbeats make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. He is master of storms and a power of the sky world, associated with the winter ceremonial realm, and his younger sibling Kolus, a downy being who sheds his coat to become human, acts as an ancestor and go-between.
source: First Arts / Simon Dick (Kanaka Bar); U'mista Cultural Society; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Tseiqami (Tse-qami) is the Kwakwaka'wakw thunderbird; the Kolus relationship (younger sibling) is documented by U'mista and First Arts. The record's 'battles the underworld serpent and controls the weather' is a fair gloss of the thunderbird complex, though the specific serpent-battle is generic across Northwest Coast thunderbird tales rather than a distinct Kwakwaka'wakw episode found here.

description: The Salmon Chief is the ruler of the salmon people, who in Northwest Coast belief don salmon coats each season. In the story recorded by Boas, a fisherman releases a talking salmon chief and is repaid with fortune; when he fails to keep the salmon bones, the chief's daughter tells him the bones are babies. The tale underlies the first-salmon rite and respect for the run.
source: Franz Boas, 'Tlingit Myths and Texts' (1917), story 51 (The Salmon Chief)
research_notes: Attested, with attribution care. The fully recorded text is Tlingit (Boas, 'The Salmon Chief,' collected at Wrangell). Tsimshian attribution is plausible and the salmon-people / salmon-chief motif and first-salmon ceremonies are shared across the Northwest Coast, but no distinct Tsimshian text of 'The Salmon Chief' was located. Flagged for culture-field care; consider describing the figure as pan-Northwest-Coast.

description: Alhkw'ntam is the supreme creator of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, the 'heavenly father' who keeps the sun in a box in Nusmata, the land above. In the Smayusta of the Four Carpenters he is served by four supernatural carpenters who carve the first ancestors, and his light is stolen by the charcoal-made Raven Qwaxw, who brings day to the world.
source: Nuxalk Nation (nuxalk.net), Smayusta: Four Carpenters
research_notes: Attested. Alhkw'ntam ('our heavenly father') is the Nuxalk creator who held the sun in a box in Nusmata; the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw) carved the First Ancestors, and Raven (Qwaxw) was made from charcoal by the youngest carpenter and tricked Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina to bring light (nuxalk.net). The record's 'made the world firm and established laws' matches the creator's role.

description: Kolus is the younger sibling of the Kwakwaka'wakw thunderbird Tseiqami, a supernatural bird who wears a coat of thick white down instead of feathers. The down makes him so warm that he sweats, sheds the coat, and becomes human; a Kolus who flew down from the sky and removed his costume became a founding ancestor, and he helps raise ceremonial house beams.
source: U'mista Cultural Society, 'Living Tradition'; First Arts / Simon Dick; Franz Boas, 'Kwakiutl Tales'
research_notes: Attested, expert-sourced. Kolus (Kulus) is the younger brother/sister of Thunderbird Tseiqami, documented by U'mista Cultural Society and Boas: thick white down instead of feathers, sheds it to become human, flies down from heaven to found clans, helps raise big-house beams. Corrected: the record's 'immense thunderbird creating thunder' is wrong for Kolus. Note: duplicate of batch-18 'kulus-kwakwaka-wakw' (same figure, alternate spelling) - merge-aware handling recommended.

description: Qwaxw is the Raven of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, made from charcoal by the youngest of the Four Carpenters, who cried 'qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw' when he came to life. He flew up to Nusmata, tricked the granddaughter of the creator, and carried away the box of daylight, so that the world below gained light, fire, and abundance.
source: Nuxalk Nation (nuxalk.net), Smayusta: Four Carpenters and Other Stories
research_notes: Attested. Qwaxw is the Nuxalk Raven who was named when the youngest of the Four Carpenters made him from charcoal and he cried 'qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw'; he tricked Alhkw'ntam to bring light, and Raven, Eagle, Grizzly Bear, and Killer Whale cloaks became ancestor crests (nuxalk.net). The record's 'brought daylight, fire, and salmon' broadly matches the light-bringing role.

description: In the Lushootseed tales of the southern Coast Salish, Crow is a clever, stubborn talker who gets the better of others by sheer will. In 'Crow and her Seagull Slaves' she lords it over the birds she has caught, while in 'Crow and the Octopus' the crab and the clam warn her away from the beach, and she answers 'I already know!'
source: Tulalip Lushootseed (tulaliplushootseed.com); told by Martha Lamont
research_notes: Attested. Tulalip Lushootseed materials document Crow as a clever, self-willed figure in 'Crow and her Seagull Slaves' (adapted from Martha Lamont) and 'Crow and the Octopus,' where crab and clam warn her and she replies 'I already know!' The record's 'clever trickster appearing alongside Raven' is a fair gloss of her talkative, headstrong role.

description: Andaokut is the hero of a Nuu-chah-nulth myth cycle who frees the children stolen by Malahas, the Woman of the Woods. He is born from the mucus or tears of the grieving mother, grows swiftly, finds the children in the forest, kills Malahas, and restores them to their families, ending the terror the ogre-woman had brought to the villages.
source: Wikipedia 'Nuu-chah-nulth mythology' (Andaokut)
research_notes: Attested. Andaokut is documented in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology as the being born from a woman's mucus (or tears) whose children Malahas stole; he rescued the children and killed Malahas. Corrected: the record's claim that he is 'an ocean spirit honored by whale hunters' is unsupported by the sources found and appears to be AI embellishment; flagged for removal.

description: Dâyuni'sï, 'Beaver's Grandchild,' is the water-beetle who plays the decisive role in the Cherokee creation story of how the world was made. When all was water, the animals sent divers down to find earth; each failed until Dâyuni'sï dove to the bottom and returned with a little mud, which spread and grew into the land.
source: James Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee' (1900), 'How the World Was Made'
research_notes: Attested; corrected. The record's generic 'Cherokee cosmology' text could be mistaken for the Little People. The attested Dâyuni'sï ('Beaver's Grandchild') is the great water-beetle earth-diver of Cherokee creation (Mooney, 'How the World Was Made'). The Little People are a separate figure (Tsundige'wï, Mooney story 74).

description: Sgaana, in Haida belief, are the supernatural beings of the sea, and the killer whale is their visible form in this world. Chiefs among the undersea people, the killer whales live in great houses beneath the ocean, rule the sea creatures, and can take human shape. The word and image figure in Haida crests and in Bill Reid's sculpture Skaana.
source: Bill Reid Centre (SFU); ACI-ICA, 'Skaana - Killer Whale, Chief of the Undersea World' (1984)
research_notes: Attested. Haida skaana means 'spirit being'; the killer whale is the visible form of the spirit world beneath the sea and is reckoned a chief among the undersea beings. Bill Reid's 1984 sculpture 'Skaana - Killer Whale, Chief of the Undersea World' reflects this. The record's 'assists worthy hunters' is not specifically documented; the chiefly/undersea role is.

description: In the Nuxalk Smayusta of Ista, First Born (Patsallht) marries a beautiful woman in a red blanket who builds him a home of hemlock. She often disappears for days, and while away she reverts to her true shape, a grizzly bear. Learning that his wife is a bear, First Born leaves her, and she never again takes human form.
source: Nuxalk Nation (nuxalk.net), Smayusta: The Story of Ista; 'From Story to Stewardship' (Zenodo)
research_notes: Attested. The Nuxalk 'Story of Ista' (nuxalk.net; quoted in the Zenodo paper 'From Story to Stewardship') tells of First Born (Patsallht) who married a grizzly-bear woman: she built a hemlock house, disappeared for days reverted to bear form, and was left when discovered. The record's 'marries a human man and teaches respect' is close; the explicit teaching-of-respect is a conservation-focused framing.

description: Iktomi is the spider trickster of the Lakota, Dakota, and Nakota peoples, a wily, foolish being whose schemes usually go wrong. His stories are told as negative models: they show what not to do and teach lessons about pride, greed, and deception through his endless failures, making him one of the best-known figures of Plains oral tradition.
source: native-languages.org (Iktomi); Wikipedia 'Iktomi'
research_notes: Attested. Iktomi is the spider trickster of the Lakota/Dakota/Nakota (Sioux), documented in extensive story cycles; he is a buffoon and negative role model whose foolish schemes teach cautionary lessons. The record's summary (central to Lakota oral tradition, teaches moral lessons, resembles other spider tricksters) is accurate.

description: In the Tlingit story of the Salmon Box (Kudatan Kahidi), Xanaax.atwaayaa is a being who holds a staff tipped with a supernatural octopus tentacle. Raven, disguised, trades him a magic arrow in the form of a magpie and gains the staff, whose power he uses to draw the salmon close to shore and to control their coming.
source: ANKN/UAF curriculum, 'Kudatan Kahidi (The Salmon Box)'
research_notes: Attested; corrected. The record described Xanaax as 'clan spirit guardians in crests and totem poles,' which is unsupported. In the ANKN/UAF legend 'Kudatan Kahidi (The Salmon Box),' Xanaax.atwaayaa owns an octopus-tentacle staff of supernatural power; Raven trades his magpie-disguised arrow for it and pulls the salmon shoreward. Not the land otter, which is kóoshdaa (kóoshdaa kaa).

description: Dzunukwa, the Wild Woman of the Woods, is a giantess of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition with a black face and sunken cheeks. She steals children and is feared as an ogress, yet she is also enormously wealthy and powerful, and the red-cedar bark she favors gives ritual strength. Her image appears in masks, the winter ceremonial world, and the art of Emily Carr.
source: U'mista Cultural Society; Franz Boas, 'Kwakiutl Tales'; Emily Carr, 'Klee Wyck'
research_notes: Attested, expert-sourced. Dzunukwa (Dzônokwa) is the Wild Woman of the Woods, a black-faced, sunken-cheeked giantess who steals children; she is also associated with great wealth and red-cedar bark, and appears in Kwakwaka'wakw masks and Emily Carr's writing and painting. The record's summary is accurate. She is not an exclusively 'cannibal' figure in all contexts, though child-stealing is core.

description: In Tsimshian and neighboring Northwest Coast tradition, the Bear People are a chiefly society who live in houses like humans and put on bear coats to travel as animals. The Bear Mother story tells how a woman who disrespected the bears was taken and married into the bear village, bore twin cubs, and how the bear chief taught the rituals of respect hunters still follow.
source: SFU Bill Reid Centre (Bear Mother); Franz Boas, 'Tsimshian Mythology'
research_notes: Attested. The Bear Mother story is documented among the Coast Tsimshian, Gitxsan, Nisga'a, and Haida (SFU Bill Reid Centre), and Boas's Tsimshian Mythology includes the Bear Mother and clan-beginning complex. The record's 'bear society with human-like houses' matches the bear village with chiefs. Emphasizes honoring animals, transformation, and travel between worlds.

description: Dukʷibəɫ, the Changer, is the transformer of Lushootseed and Coast Salish tradition who travelled the myth-age world remaking its beings. He met Blue Heron splitting cedar with his head, straightened out the chaotic creatures of that age, and left animals, rocks, and landmarks in their present forms. In other Salish languages he appears as Xelas or the Transformer Brothers.
source: Puyallup Tribal Language Program; Wikipedia 'Transformer (spirit-being)'
research_notes: Attested. 'Duk-ib' is a rendering of Lushootseed Dukʷibəɫ, the Changer, documented in the Puyallup text 'Changer and Blue Heron.' The transformer complex is shared across Coast Salish groups (Lummi Xelas/Xeʼlas, Squamish Xáays, Halkomelem Xaːls). The record's 'changed the chaotic beings of the mythic age' matches the transformer cycle.

description: In the Tsimshian tale recorded by Boas, Porcupine is a small, weak animal who turns the tables on Great-Grizzly-Bear. Burned and mocked by the proud bear, Porcupine walks off singing, and his song summons a bitter wind that freezes the land, sealing the bear in his den and killing him. The tale explains why porcupines' backs look scorched and warns against cruelty.
source: Franz Boas, 'Tsimshian Texts' (1902), story 5 (The Story of the Porcupine)
research_notes: Attested. Boas's Tsimshian Texts story 5 'The Story of the Porcupine' documents Porcupine's revenge on Great-Grizzly-Bear: burned on the back, he sings to bring ice and freezing wind, and the bear dies in his den. A companion tale, 'The Porcupine and the Beaver' (Nass River dialect), has Porcupine trick the Beaver to death in a tree-climbing game. The record's 'quills and cunning' gloss fits the cunning-over-brute-force theme.

description: Tenga is the earth goddess of the Mossi (Moose) people of Burkina Faso, wife of Wende, the supreme sky god. She is the guardian of the land, its fields, and its fertility, and authority over the earth belongs to her; humans direct their prayers through Tenga to reach Wende. She is central to Mossi ideas of land, farming, and chieftaincy.
source: denkyema.com, Moaaga philosophy (after Michel Izard)
research_notes: Attested. In Mossi (Moose/Moaaga) belief, Tenga is the earth goddess and wife of Wende, the sky god; humans reach Wende through Tenga (denkyema.com on Moaaga philosophy, citing Michel Izard). The record's 'goddess associated with field' is a thin but fair gloss of her role as guardian of land and fertility.

description: Not independently attested in Senegalese folklore. No published source records a Senegalese bush spirit named Tidzi; searches return only Tidzi, a rural commune in Essaouira Province, Morocco, and related place names. The claim that a 'Senegalese bush spirit tests travelers' resembles the Rab spirits of Wolof and Lebou belief, but no such entity named Tidzi is documented.
source: None found; see research notes
research_notes: Unattested. Searches for 'Tidzi' produce only a Moroccan toponym (Tidzi commune, Essaouira province) and related arganeraie region place names (also 'Tizi,' a Berber word for mountain pass). No Senegalese spirit of this name exists in accessible sources. Likely AI-generated or a name-conflation. Closest real analogues for a bush spirit testing travelers in Senegal: the Rab (Wolof/Lebou) or Serer bush genies; recommend repurpose or removal.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure. The source record is a generic placeholder whose description text concerns Kiowa tradition, a Native American Plains culture, while the country field says Ghana, so the record appears to have been filled by error. In Ghana the archetypal trickster is Anansi, the spider of Akan folklore, to which this entry likely refers.
source: None; see research notes
research_notes: Unattested as written. The cultural_significance text ('Important cultural figure in Kiowa tradition') is a copy-paste from a Kiowa record and contradicts the Ghana country field; the entry is a generic 'Trickster' placeholder. No distinct Ghanaian trickster beyond Anansi exists. Recommend merging with 'anansi-ghana' or removing this corrupted record. The correct Ghanaian trickster figure is Kwaku Ananse.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure. The source record is a generic placeholder that repeats text about Kiowa tradition while labelled Nigeria, an apparent copy-paste error. In Nigerian folklore the classic tricksters are the tortoise (Ijapa among the Yoruba, Mbe among the Igbo) and Gizo the spider in Hausa tales; no separate 'Trickster' entity exists.
source: None; see research notes
research_notes: Unattested as written. Same copy-paste corruption as 'trickster-ghana' (text mentions Kiowa tradition while country says Nigeria). The record is a generic placeholder. Actual Nigerian trickster figures: Ijapa (Yoruba tortoise), Mbe/Mbeku (Igbo tortoise), Gizo (Hausa spider). Recommend removing the placeholder or repurposing to the tortoise trickster tradition.

description: In Dogon cosmology the turtle carries an ancient significance tied to the structure of the world. Marcel Griaule recorded a Dogon conception in which the hexagonal plates of the turtle's shell mirror the sacred layout of the cosmos, and secondary retellings picture the earth on the back of a giant turtle beneath a sky held by four pillars. The image links land, order, and spirits.
source: Marcel Griaule (cited in MAA journal 1948/1980); secondary retellings of the Dogon creation
research_notes: Partially attested. Scholarly support exists: Griaule recorded Dogon turtle symbolism in which the shell's hexagonal plates mirror cosmic/sacred space (Griaule 1948:128; 1980:123, as cited in the MAA journal). The 'giant turtle supporting the earth' framing appears mainly in popular retellings (e.g., Memory Wizards) and is not an established academic reading of Dogon cosmology; flagged as fair/derivative. Country: Mali (Bandiagara).

description: Not independently attested as a central Ashanti trickster. In Akan tradition the trickster par excellence is Anansi, the spider, who wins the stories from the sky god Nyame; tortoise figures appear in some Akan tales but hold no such role. The tortoise-as-trickster is the classic figure of Yoruba and Igbo folklore in Nigeria, suggesting this entry conflates Anansi with the West African tortoise.
source: None found; see research notes
research_notes: Unattested. The Ashanti/Akan trickster is Anansi the spider (Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales); the tortoise is not a central Ashanti trickster figure. The tortoise trickster is documented among the Yoruba (Ijapa) and Igbo (Mbe) of Nigeria, and in some pan-West-African tortoise tales. This entry likely conflates Anansi with the West African tortoise; recommend repurpose to the Yoruba/Igbo tortoise or remove.

description: Anansi, called Kwaku Ananse, is the spider trickster of the Akan and Ashanti peoples of Ghana, a small creature who overcomes mighty foes by wit. In the best-known tale he wins the sky god Nyame's stories by capturing the python Onini, the hornets Mmoboro, the leopard Osebo, and the dwarf Mmoatia, after which all tales are called anansesem.
source: R. S. Rattray, 'Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales' (1930); Britannica 'Ananse'; Wikipedia 'Anansi'
research_notes: Attested, richly documented. Kwaku Ananse is the Akan/Ashanti spider trickster; the story of winning Nyame's stories by capturing Onini the python, Mmoboro the hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the dwarf is recorded by Rattray and widely retold. 'Kwaku' is the Akan day-name for a boy born on Wednesday. Anansesem ('spider tales') names the whole Ghanaian tale genre.

description: In the Ivory Coast, the spider trickster of the Akan appears as Kacou Ananzè among the Baoule and other Akan peoples, who carry the same story cycle across the border from Ghana. Kacou, like Kwaku, is the day-name of a boy born on Wednesday, and his tales of outwitting larger beasts, gods, and neighbours belong to the shared anansesem tradition.
source: Wikipedia 'Anansi' (variant list); Akan oral tradition (Baoule/Anyi)
research_notes: Attested. The Akan are a trans-border people spanning Ghana and Ivory Coast; the Baoule and Anyi of the Ivory Coast carry the spider trickster as Kacou Ananzè, Kacou being the Wednesday day-name cognate of Kwaku (Wikipedia Anansi variant list). The figure is the same anansesem cycle. The record's 'Akan/Ashanti folklore... spread via slave trade' is accurate.
